title: My Calendar I
description: Brute force to optimized: checking a new booking against every existing one versus a sorted structure that only needs to check the two nearest neighbors.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Design a class representing a calendar that supports book(start, end), adding a new event covering [start, end). Return true if the event can be added without overlapping any existing event, and false otherwise (in which case it is not added).

blocks.text: Maintain a growing set of non-overlapping booked intervals. For each new booking request, accept it (and keep it) only if it does not overlap any existing booking.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Single Meeting Room That Cannot Double-Book
blocks.text: Picture a single meeting room booking system where no two meetings are allowed to overlap. Each new request is only approved if it does not conflict with any meeting already on the calendar.

blocks.caption: Keeping bookings sorted lets a search narrow to just the neighbors that could overlap

blocks.text: book(10,20) is accepted (true); book(15,25) overlaps [10,20) and is rejected (false); book(20,30) starts exactly where [10,20) ends, no overlap, accepted (true). Results: [true, false, true].
Before checking a new booking against every existing one, notice that keeping bookings sorted by start time means only a couple of neighboring bookings could possibly overlap the new one.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Two intervals [s1, e1) and [s2, e2) overlap exactly when s1 is less than e2 AND s2 is less than e1.

Observation 2: If existing bookings are kept sorted by start time, the only bookings that could possibly overlap a new [start, end) are the one starting just before it, and the one starting just after it.

Observation 3: A binary search (or a balanced search tree / sorted map) finds those neighboring bookings in O(log n), rather than scanning every existing booking.

Observation 4: Checking overlap against just those 1 or 2 neighbors is enough to correctly decide whether the new booking can be added.
This leads to maintaining bookings in a sorted structure by start time, and using a search to check only the relevant neighbors for overlap, instead of every existing booking.
Keep bookings in a plain list. For each new booking, check it directly against every existing booking for overlap.

items: For every existing booking, check whether it overlaps the new [start, end).
If any overlap is found, reject the new booking (return false).
If no overlap is found with any existing booking, add the new booking to the list and return true.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check the new booking against every existing one directly

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every existing booking is checked directly, in whatever order they happen to be stored.
The overlap condition, start less than the other's end AND the other's start less than end, is applied identically for every comparison.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) per booking, checking every existing one; O(n squared) across n calls total.
Space: O(n) for the stored bookings.

Limitation: most of the existing bookings could not possibly overlap a given new one, only the ones with nearby start times are actually relevant; checking every single one wastes effort as the calendar grows.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every booking is wasteful: if bookings are kept sorted by start time, only the booking immediately before and immediately after the new one's start time could possibly overlap it.

What structure supports fast neighbor lookup: a sorted map or balanced search tree keyed by start time, supporting O(log n) insertion and O(log n) "find the neighbor" queries.

The core idea: find the booking with the largest start time that is still less than or equal to the new booking's start (the "floor"), and the booking with the smallest start time greater than it (the "ceiling"), and check overlap against only those two.

Maintain bookings in a sorted map keyed by start time. For a new [start, end), find the floor entry (the closest existing booking starting at or before start) and check whether its end exceeds start; find the ceiling entry (the closest existing booking starting after start) and check whether its start is less than end. If neither overlaps, insert the new booking and return true.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: binary search for the two possible neighbors, check only those

blocks.text: Since bookings are kept sorted by start time, any booking that could possibly overlap a new [start, end) must be either the one immediately before it (whose end might extend past start) or the one immediately after it (whose start might be before end). No booking further away in either direction can overlap, since sorted order guarantees everything else is either entirely before or entirely after those two neighbors. Checking just those two is therefore sufficient, and finding them takes only O(log n) in a sorted map.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n) per booking.
Space: O(n) for the sorted map of bookings.

blocks.text: My Calendar I shows how keeping data sorted turns an "overlap check against everything" problem into an "overlap check against just the nearest neighbors" problem, answerable with a fast search instead of a full scan.

items: Using a strict less-than-or-equal check for overlap instead of strict less-than, which would incorrectly reject bookings that only touch at their boundary.
Checking only one neighbor (just before, or just after) instead of both.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating the overlap condition (start1 < end2 and start2 < end1) up front, and then explaining why sorted order limits the relevant comparisons to just two neighbors, demonstrates the full reasoning clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every existing booking", think: keep bookings sorted by start time, and only the immediate neighbors could possibly overlap.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n) time per call. The optimized sorted-map approach runs in O(log n) time per call. Both use O(n) space.

items: Pattern: a sorted structure (by start time), reducing an overlap check to just the nearest neighbors.
Core Idea: only the booking immediately before and immediately after a new booking's start time could possibly overlap it; check just those two.
Time: O(n) per call for the brute force, O(log n) per call for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: sorted order limits which existing bookings can possibly overlap a new one to just its immediate neighbors.
Interview Difficulty: a clean introduction to sorted-structure-based interval management.
One line memory trick: keep bookings sorted; only the neighbors can possibly overlap.
